Every rule the program ships, in the words the program shows. A rule says which observations are worth
showing and what they can show. It never decides that someone cheated. Each result is **Found**, **Not
found** together with how far back its source can see, or **Not measured** together with a reason, and
beside every Found row the program shows the ordinary things that also produce it.

A report header shows its rule count and bundle SHA-256. A report with a different SHA-256 came from a
program with a different set of rules: read this page at the commit that program was built from.

## How to read a rule

- **Matches when** lists conditions on one observation, something a collector saw. All of them must
  hold. Text is compared without regard to ASCII case unless the condition says it is compared
  exactly.
- If the collector could not read a field a condition names, the rule is **Not measured**, never Not
  found.
- **Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines** lists the reasons the rule's
  author said carry no information on such a machine. SS mode counts them instead of listing them (ADR 0027).
- **Strength** says what the evidence can show: `execution`, a program ran; `presence`, a file or
  program existed; `tamper`, traces were removed or altered; `posture`, a machine setting that makes
  cheating easier; `context`, background for the reviewer.

Writing or changing a rule: [rules-authoring.md](rules-authoring.md). Checking a PC over a
screenshare: [screenshare-guide.md](screenshare-guide.md).

## Collector `evtx`

### `evtx` / `log-clearing`

<a id="rule-f4c99b57-02c8-4e53-82d0-dba8bdc13dda"></a>

#### An event log file was cleared

- Id: `f4c99b57-02c8-4e53-82d0-dba8bdc13dda`
- File: [`rules/evtx/log-clearing/event-log-file-cleared/rule.yaml`](../rules/evtx/log-clearing/event-log-file-cleared/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `evtx`
- Strength: `tamper`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `evtx`, `log-clearing`
- Written: 2026-09-13

**About this check**

The System log holds a record saying an event log file was cleared, with the time it happened. Windows names the cleared log inside that record, and this tool does not read record contents, so it cannot say which of the PC's several hundred logs this was, and most of them hold nothing a reviewer would care about. The count shown with this row is how many such records survive, and a high one is not a worse finding: clearing every log at once, in a second, is what one click of a PC "optimiser" does, so a large number is evidence for that explanation rather than against it. A clearing of the Security log can be recorded here as well as there, so this row and "The Security log records that it was cleared" can be one action rather than two.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `channel`: is `System` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `event_id`: is `104`
- `provider`: is `Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only clearings still recorded in the System log as it stands today. The log holds a limited window and overwrites its oldest records, and clearing the System log removes these records along with everything else — so nothing found here does not mean no log was ever cleared.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `not_admin` — Windows would not show this without administrator rights
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Gaming "optimiser", "debloat" and "tweak" scripts. Several popular ones clear every log on the PC in one click, which is why the count here reaches the hundreds, and the owner has usually forgotten running one months ago
- A prebuilt or repaired PC. The factory imaging step Windows itself provides deletes the event logs, so the maker, not the owner, cleared them
- Installing software that resets the local event log as part of its setup — monitoring and support agents commonly do
- The owner, a shop or a friend clicking "Clear Log" in Event Viewer while chasing a crash, which is standard troubleshooting advice and can be done while keeping a backup copy
- A Windows feature update or in-place reinstall, and routine maintenance scripts and scheduled tasks that tidy logs on a timer

**Related rules**

- similar to [The Security log records that it was cleared](#rule-ff967b28-984b-4de0-b361-58367ae0c2d5)

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/wevtutil>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/manufacture/desktop/sysprep-command-line-options>
- <https://github.com/SigmaHQ/sigma/blob/master/rules/windows/builtin/system/microsoft_windows_eventlog/win_system_eventlog_cleared.yml>

<a id="rule-ff967b28-984b-4de0-b361-58367ae0c2d5"></a>

#### The Security log records that it was cleared

- Id: `ff967b28-984b-4de0-b361-58367ae0c2d5`
- File: [`rules/evtx/log-clearing/security-audit-log-cleared/rule.yaml`](../rules/evtx/log-clearing/security-audit-log-cleared/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `evtx`
- Strength: `tamper`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `evtx`, `log-clearing`
- Written: 2026-09-13

**About this check**

The Security log holds a record saying the security audit log was cleared, with the time it happened. Windows writes that record whatever the audit settings are, so it is the log's own account of itself. It does not say who cleared it, why, or what the log held before — this tool reads the file and not the record's details, and whatever was there is gone. Clearing a log is something a great many ordinary tools and people do, and the list beside this row is not a formality: read it. Clearing the Security log can also be recorded a second time in the System log, so this row and "An event log file was cleared" can be one action rather than two.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `channel`: is `Security` (text, ASCII case ignored)
- `event_id`: is `1102`
- `provider`: is `Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Only clearings still recorded in the Security log as it stands today. The log holds a limited window and overwrites its oldest records, and a later clearing removes the record of an earlier one — so nothing found here does not mean no log was ever cleared.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `not_admin` — Windows would not show this without administrator rights
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- Gaming "optimiser", "debloat" and "tweak" scripts. Several popular ones clear every log on the PC in one click, months before any of this, and the owner has usually forgotten running one
- A prebuilt or repaired PC. The factory imaging step Windows itself provides deletes the event logs, so the maker, not the owner, cleared this log
- Installing software that resets the local event log as part of its setup — monitoring and support agents commonly do
- The owner, a shop or a friend clicking "Clear Log" in Event Viewer while chasing a crash, which is standard troubleshooting advice and can be done while keeping a backup copy
- A Windows feature update or in-place reinstall, and routine maintenance scripts and scheduled tasks that tidy logs on a timer

**Related rules**

- similar to [An event log file was cleared](#rule-f4c99b57-02c8-4e53-82d0-dba8bdc13dda)

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/event-1102>
- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/auditing/other-events>

## Collector `posture`

### `posture` / `boot`

<a id="rule-7c1f3a52-9d4e-4b8a-a6f2-3e5d9b0c41e7"></a>

#### Secure Boot is turned off

- Id: `7c1f3a52-9d4e-4b8a-a6f2-3e5d9b0c41e7`
- File: [`rules/posture/boot/secure-boot-disabled/rule.yaml`](../rules/posture/boot/secure-boot-disabled/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `posture`
- Strength: `posture`
- Status: `test` — believed correct; has a positive and a negative fixture
- Tags: `posture`, `boot`
- Written: 2026-09-11

**About this check**

Windows reports that UEFI Secure Boot is off. Secure Boot only lets signed boot loaders and early drivers start; with it off, unsigned low-level software is easier to load. Many ordinary PCs run with it off, so on its own this describes the machine — it is not evidence of cheating.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `secure_boot`: is `disabled` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Current setting only. It says nothing about how the PC was configured in the past.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- PCs that boot in legacy BIOS or CSM mode, or were never switched to Secure Boot
- Dual-boot setups with operating systems that need it off
- Owners who turned it off for hardware, virtualisation or overclocking tools

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/design/device-experiences/oem-secure-boot>

<a id="rule-75162c70-a6d1-47ec-94af-be25184d5ece"></a>

#### Windows test signing is turned on

- Id: `75162c70-a6d1-47ec-94af-be25184d5ece`
- File: [`rules/posture/boot/test-signing-enabled/rule.yaml`](../rules/posture/boot/test-signing-enabled/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `posture`
- Strength: `posture`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `posture`, `boot`
- Written: 2026-09-12

**About this check**

Windows reports that test signing is on, so the kernel also starts drivers that no trusted publisher signed, including self-signed ones. That lowers the bar for loading kernel-level software of any kind. It is a setting the owner of the machine chose, and several ordinary kinds of work need it, so on its own this describes the machine — it is not evidence of cheating.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `test_signing`: is `enabled` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Current setting only. It says nothing about how the PC was configured in the past.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- People who write or test their own drivers, for whom this is a normal working setting
- Hardware and firmware engineers using vendor or pre-release tools
- Software whose own installation instructions ask the owner to switch test signing on

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-hardware/drivers/install/the-testsigning-boot-configuration-option>

### `posture` / `memory-integrity`

<a id="rule-8458638a-04fd-4bbf-910a-c4dd9bbe36bb"></a>

#### Memory integrity (HVCI) is configured off

- Id: `8458638a-04fd-4bbf-910a-c4dd9bbe36bb`
- File: [`rules/posture/memory-integrity/hvci-disabled/rule.yaml`](../rules/posture/memory-integrity/hvci-disabled/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `posture`
- Strength: `posture`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `posture`, `memory-integrity`
- Written: 2026-09-12

**About this check**

Windows is configured not to enforce Hypervisor-Enforced Code Integrity, so kernel code is not checked inside the hypervisor-protected environment that feature provides. This reads the configured policy and not a live confirmation that the hypervisor is enforcing anything: a PC whose hardware lacks the necessary virtualisation support can carry the setting either way and enforce nothing. Memory integrity is off on a great many ordinary PCs, so on its own this describes the machine — it is not evidence of cheating.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `hvci`: is `disabled` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Current setting only. It says nothing about how the PC was configured in the past.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `source_absent` — this PC has no such record to read
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- PCs whose hardware or firmware cannot support virtualisation-based security
- Machines where it was switched off to resolve a driver, anti-cheat or virtualisation conflict
- The many consumer PCs, and PCs upgraded in place, that simply run with it off by default

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/hardware-security/enable-virtualization-based-protection-of-code-integrity>

### `posture` / `tpm`

<a id="rule-66d513b5-fe61-415a-9385-9d01f85c3ef5"></a>

#### No TPM is present

- Id: `66d513b5-fe61-415a-9385-9d01f85c3ef5`
- File: [`rules/posture/tpm/tpm-absent/rule.yaml`](../rules/posture/tpm/tpm-absent/rule.yaml)
- Collector: `posture`
- Strength: `context`
- Status: `experimental` — being developed
- Tags: `posture`, `tpm`
- Written: 2026-09-12

**About this check**

The platform reports that this machine has no TPM. A TPM is one of the stable pieces of hardware an identity can be tied to, so whether one exists is useful background when a reviewer is reading the rest of a report. Enormous numbers of working PCs have no TPM at all or have it switched off in firmware, so this says nothing about the person using the machine and is not evidence of cheating.

**Matches when all of these hold for one observation**

- `tpm`: is `absent` (text, ASCII case ignored)

**Look-back**

Current hardware state only. It says nothing about earlier hardware or firmware settings.

**Not measured, and named by the rule as ordinary on some machines**

- `not_windows` — not running on Windows
- `access_denied` — Windows refused to open this

**Ordinary things that also produce this**

- PCs built without a TPM, which includes a great many older and self-assembled machines
- A TPM switched off or hidden in firmware, which is a common factory default
- Virtual machines and test systems that have no virtual TPM attached

**References**

- <https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/hardware-security/tpm/trusted-platform-module-overview>
